title: How Ocean Currents Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain ocean currents: what they are, why they persist or change, and the main types. Covered are coastal and longshore currents created by wind-driven waves, rip currents formed by sandbar gaps, upwelling and downwelling and their role in nutrient and oxygen exchange, surface currents driven by wind, heat and the Coriolis effect, the five major gyres (including the Gulf Stream, named by Ben Franklin), the Ekman spiral, the deep-ocean thermohaline global conveyor belt driven by cold dense salty water, the Mediterranean outflow used by World War Two submarines, tidal currents (flood and ebb), and climate change threats to the conveyor belt and El Nino. The episode closes with a listener mail about the heavy metal music interludes.

segments.title: Opening banter and tire store tangent
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about the episode topic, ocean currents, then digress into a long joke about rain driving and tire stores.

segments.title: Ancient currents and purpose of currents
segments.summary: Currents change over time; some, like the Gulf Stream, have existed about five million years since the Isthmus of Panama formed. Currents support marine life by carrying nutrients, with phytoplankton as the base of the food chain.

segments.title: Surface currents, coastal currents and longshore current
segments.summary: Surface currents are wind-driven and make up about ten percent of ocean water. Coastal currents come from waves, which come from wind, which comes from heat at the equator. Waves hitting the shore at an angle create a longshore current that moves sand and sediment along the beach.

segments.title: Rip currents and riptides
segments.summary: Longshore drift builds sandbars and spits that block returning waves. A break in a sandbar acts as a funnel, creating a rip current that can pull swimmers out to sea and is dangerous even for strong swimmers.

segments.title: Upwelling and downwelling
segments.summary: When wind pushes surface water away from shore, deeper water rises to replace it, which is upwelling. Surface water is oxygen rich and low in nutrients, while deep water is cold, nutrient rich and high in CO2. The exchange moves oxygen downward and nutrients upward, sustaining marine life such as the life in Antarctica.

segments.title: Coriolis effect, ocean topography and gyres
segments.summary: Heat at the equator, plus the Earth's rotation and the Coriolis effect, curves winds and surface currents. Wind mounds water into hills a few feet tall; the Coriolis effect turns the water around these mounds, forming five major gyres: North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific and Indian Ocean.

segments.title: Gulf Stream, Ekman spiral and Ben Franklin
segments.summary: The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre, moving about fifteen Superdomes of water per second and warming Western Europe and the US East Coast climate. The Ekman spiral describes how water below the surface moves against wind. Ben Franklin, as Postmaster General, charted the Gulf Stream in the eighteenth century to explain slower mail from England.
